explanations.explanation: I wish it went that way, friend, but cheers aren't what the text says. It says they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit (Luke 24:37). Nobody throws confetti at a ghost. They were stunned, and I think that's about how I'd look if my cookie jar started talking.

Right, friend, no cheers yet. The text says they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit. Jesus walks in saying "Peace be with you," and the room goes quiet, not loud. I think a few of them stopped breathing for a second.

Yes, baker, a spirit is what they thought they were looking at. The text says they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit. Jesus answers that guess right away in the next verses. He's got hands, feet, flesh and bones to show them.

Close to a holy word, but not what the text says, baker. A prophet would be a person standing there with a message. The text says they were startled and frightened, thinking they had seen a spirit. That's why Jesus has so much to show them in the verses that follow.

A stranger would've been a little scary, baker, but it's not what they guessed. The text says they thought they had seen a spirit. These are people who knew Jesus, and still the first thing they thought was ghost. Their minds went somewhere wild, and I can't say I'd do better.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "Touch Me and see…" (Luke 24:39). He doesn't just talk His way out of the confusion. He invites them to check for themselves. A man who tells you to touch Him has nothing to hide.
It's True, friend, and here's the proof. Jesus says, "Touch Me and see…" (Luke 24:39). He wasn't shy about it. He wanted the doubt gone, and He gave them a way to check it for themselves.

explanations.answer: A spirit has no flesh and bones
explanations.explanation: That's the reason, baker. Jesus says, "…for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have." (Luke 24:39). He's pointing at what's right there in front of them. A ghost can't be touched, and He tells them to touch Him.

explanations.answer: His touch will calm their fear
explanations.explanation: That's a sweet thought, friend, but Jesus doesn't say it. He gives a different reason: "…for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have." (Luke 24:39). Maybe their fears settled down after that. I think so, but the text doesn't say. What He states is the flesh and bones.

Forgiveness does come up in this passage, baker, but not here. Here Jesus says, "…for a spirit does not have flesh and bones, as you see I have." (Luke 24:39). The touching is about showing them it's really Him. He's answering the spirit idea, plain and simple.

Yes, baker. He asks, "Do you have anything here to eat?" (Luke 24:41). Out of everything He could say in that moment, He asks about food. I respect a man who gets to the point, because that's how I feel around a fresh batch.

Not a basin, friend. The text says He asked, "Do you have anything here to eat?" (Luke 24:41). The disciples were still taking in joy and amazement. Then Jesus brings it down to something simple and ordinary.

No chair needed, baker. Jesus asks, "Do you have anything here to eat?" (Luke 24:41). He stood among them from the start, and the text never has Him ask to sit. He asks for something to eat, and that one question gets another proof going.

That's the one, baker. They gave Him a piece of broiled fish, and He took it and ate it in front of them (Luke 24:42-43). There's no ghost trick in that one. Eating in front of them is just another way of showing He's really there.

Good guess, baker, but it's not the menu. The text says they gave Him a piece of broiled fish. And He took it and ate it right in front of them. I'm a cookie guy myself, but I'll admit fish was the pick that day.

Grapes would've been fancy, friend, but the text doesn't have them. It says they gave Him a piece of broiled fish. Then He took it and ate it in front of them. Nobody can say a ghost was just standing there, because He was eating.

Oh, baker, it's the opposite, so let me set it straight. Jesus says, "Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms." (Luke 24:44). He doesn't say some of it. He says everything, and that covers all three parts of the Scriptures.

That's right, baker. Jesus says, "Everything must be fulfilled that is written about Me in the Law of Moses, the Prophets, and the Psalms." (Luke 24:44). Not a piece of it and not half. He says everything, and that's a lot of Scripture pointing one way.
That's right, baker. The text says, "Then He opened their minds to understand the Scriptures." (Luke 24:45). Understanding doesn't come from the disciples alone here. Jesus opens their minds Himself.

A scroll is a good guess for a Bible story, friend, but the text has something else. It says Jesus opened their minds to understand the Scriptures. So the opening happens inside them, not on a shelf. I think that's a gift worth more than any scroll.
No doors this time, baker. The text says Jesus opened their minds to understand the Scriptures (Luke 24:45). The temple does come up, but later, in the last verse. Here it's all about their minds.

That's it, baker. Jesus says, "…in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations, beginning in Jerusalem." (Luke 24:47). It's going out in His name, and it's going out to all nations. That's a lot of doors to knock on.

explanations.answer: A new law for every land
explanations.explanation: Not quite, friend. Jesus says, "…in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations…" (Luke 24:47). He doesn't talk about a new law here. The message is repentance and forgiveness of sins.

The temple isn't what's being proclaimed, baker. Jesus says, "…in His name repentance and forgiveness of sins will be proclaimed to all nations…" (Luke 24:47). Nothing about building anything. The word going out to the nations is repentance and forgiveness of sins.

Yes, baker, Jerusalem. Jesus says it will be proclaimed to all nations, "…beginning in Jerusalem." (Luke 24:47). That's the city where the disciples are standing right now. The starting line is right under their feet.

Galilee is a real place in the story, friend, but it's not named here. Jesus says, "…beginning in Jerusalem." (Luke 24:47). The disciples don't have to go far to find the starting line. They're already standing in that city.

Nazareth is a good guess for Jesus' story, baker, but Jesus doesn't name it here. He says, "…beginning in Jerusalem." (Luke 24:47). So that's where the message begins, in the very city where they're standing.

True, baker. Jesus tells them, "You are witnesses of these things." (Luke 24:48). They saw Him suffer and now they've seen Him alive, touched and fed. Having seen it all, they're the ones who can tell it.
It's True, friend. Jesus says, "You are witnesses of these things." (Luke 24:48). He puts it right on them, the ones who have seen it. I think that's a weighty job, and He gives it to them straight.

explanations.answer: Until they're clothed with power from on high
explanations.explanation: That's the one, baker. Jesus says, "But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high." (Luke 24:49). They're not told to start on their own strength. They're told to wait for the promise He's sending, and the waiting has a clear end.

explanations.answer: Until they've told the elders all they have seen
explanations.explanation: The elders don't show up in His instructions, friend. Jesus says, "But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high." (Luke 24:49). The waiting ends with power from on high, not with a report. I'd have been checking the oven timer the whole time.

explanations.answer: Until they've gathered every believer from Galilee
explanations.explanation: Nobody's sent on a gathering trip, baker. Jesus says, "But remain in the city until you have been clothed with power from on high." (Luke 24:49). The task is to stay put until that happens. Their job right then is to wait.

explanations.answer: He is carried up into heaven
explanations.explanation: Yes, baker. The text says, "While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven." (Luke 24:51). It happens right in the middle of the blessing. The last thing the disciples get from Him in this passage is a blessing.

explanations.answer: He sends them out two by two
explanations.explanation: Not here, friend. The text says, "While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven." (Luke 24:51). No sending out happens in this moment. The blessing is still going when He's taken up.

explanations.answer: He breaks bread with them again
explanations.explanation: No bread this time, baker. The text says, "While He was blessing them, He left them and was carried up into heaven." (Luke 24:51). He had eaten with them earlier, but at Bethany it's a blessing, and then He's carried up.

That's right, baker. The text says they were "praising God continually in the temple." (Luke 24:53). That's where this passage ends, with them back in Jerusalem and full of praise. It's a joyful place to land.

A synagogue would make sense as a place to praise, friend, but it's not what Luke says. The text says they were "praising God continually in the temple." (Luke 24:53). So that's where they were, in Jerusalem.

I'd like to see that, baker, praise breaking out between the stalls. But the text says they were "praising God continually in the temple." (Luke 24:53). They went back to Jerusalem and spent their time there in praise.
